extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers and policymakers in sociology/criminology/media studies interested in policing, race relations and news production
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance on how police organisation, police–black community relations, and journalists' 'news values' shape the construction and amplification of social problems (here: 'mugging'). Intended for sociological analysis of policing, moral panics and media selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinal news value: extraordinariness
rubrics_metrics.description: Orientation to items which are 'out of the ordinary', which in some way breach our 'normal' expectations about social life — called the primary or cardinal news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: sudden earthquake or the moon-landing. Journalists treat extraordinariness as the primary criterion when judging newsworthiness and will tend to emphasise extraordinary elements in stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: elite persons/nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Events which concern elite persons or nations score highly as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of elites increases news potential (e.g. heads of powerful nations). This is listed among the news values that structure selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic events are privileged as newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama is a routine criterion used by journalists to decide which stories to select and how to frame them.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Events which can be personalised so as to point up the essentially human characteristics of humour, sadness, sentimentality, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalisation turns abstract events into human stories, increasing their newsworthiness and editorial appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: negative consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Events which have negative consequences are judged more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative-impact stories (e.g., disasters, crimes) attract editorial attention and are prioritised.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value: thematic fit / part of existing theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Events which are part of, or can be made to appear part of, an existing newsworthy theme have greater news potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that can be linked to ongoing themes (e.g., crime waves) are more likely to be elevated to major pieces; the chapter stresses that news values operate together as a structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation-driven selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The routine organisation of newspapers (specialist correspondents, departments, institutional contacts, and the paper's structure e.g. home/foreign/political sections) predisposes them to certain types or areas of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because papers must produce news regularly, their staffing and organisational structure direct them to particular categories of events, shaping what is selected as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined news-values determine story priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that score high on a number of news-value dimensions have greater news potential; those that score high on all dimensions can become dominant items (e.g., interrupt programmes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists will play up elements that increase a story's score across values; the chapter notes that items high on multiple values become major 'lead' stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists amplify extraordinary/dramatic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and editors will tend to play up extraordinary, dramatic, or tragic elements of a story to enhance its newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an operational tendency in news production that affects selection and framing, not a formally codified rule but a widely shared professional ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police role shift: 'peace-keeper' to 'crime-fighter'
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes (amalgamation of forces, growth of squads, technological devices, motorised transport, radios) have decreased beat independence and moved the policeman from 'peace-keeper' to professional 'crime-fighter'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shift reduced cultural contact with communities, increased dependence on superiors, and altered expectations of police behaviour and status (less on-the-spot independence, more car-bound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialisation weakens police–community links
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of specialised squads (Regional Crime Squads, Special Patrol Group, anti-mugging squads) and specialisation within the force further loosened bonds between police and community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These units concentrate on specific crime types, mobilise swiftly anywhere needed, and thereby reduce the traditional friendly community ties of beat policing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special Patrol Group (SPG) characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: SPG described as an 'elite force' with its own chain of command, separate radio communications, unit mobilisation, armed officers and a 'swamping' role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SPG units acted as a 'back-up squad' and were used to 'swamp' areas experiencing increases in crime (e.g., stamping out mugging); their semi-military organisation and preparedness influenced policing style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialist squads' operational style predisposes to harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: New squads modelled on Regional Crime Squads and SPGs were organisationally committed to the specialist role and style: to expect trouble, to anticipate trouble and to take the offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given this style—far from 'delicate' handling—some degree of harassment and intimidation was described as almost inevitable in their operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police discretion shaped by 'social temperature'
rubrics_metrics.description: How, where and in what manner law is enforced (areas of police discretion) are influenced by the prevailing 'social temperature' — shifts in public feeling, anxieties and concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two contexts amplifying this effect in the period are 'law-and-order' concerns and anti-immigrant feeling; these societal contexts sensitize police to particular issues and shape enforcement priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police self-image as representatives of 'normal' citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The force tends to see itself as 'representing the desires of a hypothesized "normal" decent citizen', which informs informal policing priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This self-image mediates the policing of public order and affects discretionary decisions about enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police occupational isolation and stereotype reinforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of social segregation, police have little or no opportunity to meet coloured citizens except in contexts of professional contact, increasing susceptibility to stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This isolation gives police more opportunity and legitimacy to act on prejudices and to have them reinforced (e.g., treating 'coloured young men' differently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Police mood as an explanatory criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A prevailing police 'mood' characterised by growing impatience, frustration and anger shaped public statements and demands for harsher penal measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public declarations by senior officers and press coverage reflected and amplified this mood, influencing political discourse and possible policy shifts (e.g., calls for longer sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Police as active agents in producing moral panics
rubrics_metrics.description: Police do not simply react to moral panics; they actively participate in defining situations, selecting targets, initiating campaigns, structuring these campaigns, and selectively signifying their actions to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are part of the circle out of which moral panics develop and can inadvertently amplify the deviancy they seek to control; their 'invisibility' and pre-emptive mobilisation are important to this role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection rates and authorised strength as performance/context indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection rates (national detection rates for indictable crime fell from 49% to 39% between 1955–65) and force strength (consistently below authorised strength) are used to interpret police capacity, morale and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declining detection rates alongside rising crime volumes and staffing shortages contextualise organisational change, public sentiment and police complaints about 'losing the war against crime'.
